Both domains are classified in SCOPe as class b (all-beta), fold b.1 (immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich), superfamily b.1.2 (fibronectin type III), and family b.1.2.1 (fibronectin type III). That family assignment is the strongest evolutionary claim available here: curators judged the two to be homologous FnIII domains. The 'fragment' flag on d1o5dt2 does not weaken that assignment. What it does say is that the coordinates for this domain are incomplete. I believe d1o5dt2 is one of the two FnIII-like domains of the tissue-factor chain (chain T) in a factor VIIa/tissue factor complex, but I am recalling that from memory and have not checked it here. Either the construct was truncated or residues are missing or disordered, so the observed structure does not cover the whole domain. That should change how the domain is handled in three ways.

(1) Alignment. Do not treat the fragment as a full-length FnIII domain in a global alignment. Use local or semi-global alignment, structural or sequence, with end gaps and internal gaps at the missing segments left unpenalized. Base identity, RMSD and TM-score on the residues actually aligned. Normalize TM-score by the length of the complete partner (d1uc6a1) or report both normalizations. Otherwise a short or gapped fragment will look either falsely dissimilar (penalized for what is missing) or falsely similar (a high score from a short core alignment). Missing strands or loops can also make strand-register assignment ambiguous near the gaps. Check the alignment against the conserved FnIII seven-strand topology (A-B-E / C'-C-F-G) rather than trusting the alignment program blindly.

(2) Representative selection. When picking a family or species representative, or building ASTRAL-style nonredundant subsets and templates, prefer complete, well-resolved domains such as d1uc6a1. Use the fragment only when it is the sole example of its protein or species. ASTRAL-style quality ranking (AEROSPACI score, completeness, resolution) penalizes partial or low-quality entries for this reason. If the fragment is used as a template, the regions it lacks cannot be modelled from it. Any homology model built on it inherits the gaps, and those parts need another FnIII template or must be marked low-confidence. Also, d1o5dt2 is one domain of a multidomain chain (the '2' suffix) in a complex. Its boundaries and conformation may reflect domain splitting and interfaces with the partner protein, so it is not an ideal isolated-domain exemplar.

(3) Interpreting family diversity. Differences between d1uc6a1 and d1o5dt2 in length, missing loops or strands, lower structural similarity, or apparent loss of FnIII elements should not be read as real evolutionary divergence or new structural variation within b.1.2.1. They are artifacts of incomplete coordinates. Leave fragments out of, or flag them in, analyses of loop-length variation, core size, pairwise-distance distributions, or 'how divergent is this family'. Otherwise the family will look more heterogeneous than it is. Sequence-based diversity counts should use the full SEQRES or UniProt sequence, not the ATOM-derived fragment.

Limits:
- Membership in b.1.2.1 supports homology but not shared function. FnIII is a very large, functionally diverse family spread across extracellular-matrix proteins, receptors, cytokine receptors and tissue factor. So functions such as ligand binding, the tissue factor/FVIIa cofactor role, or whatever function the d1uc6a1 protein has should not move between these domains on the basis of family membership alone.
- Do not infer missing structure in the fragment from d1uc6a1 beyond the conserved FnIII core.
- Classification and fragment status are specific to a SCOPe release. Confirm both in the release you are using (for example SCOPe 2.07/2.08 parseable files and ASTRAL headers) and in the PDB entry's missing-residue (REMARK 465) or construct records. I have not verified them here.
